July 20 (Asia Today) -- Readily accessible deposits at South Korea's five largest banks fell by more than 41 trillion won ($27.7 billion) during the first half of July, marking their largest decline in more than six years.

The drop reflected seasonal corporate cash movements following midyear financial reporting, continued stock purchases by individual investors and a shift toward fixed-term deposits offering higher interest rates.

Demand deposits at KB Kookmin Bank, Shinhan Bank, Hana Bank, Woori Bank and NH NongHyup Bank totaled 681.09 trillion won ($457.5 billion) as of Wednesday, according to financial industry data.

The balance was down 41.2 trillion won ($27.7 billion), or 5.7%, from the end of June. It was the largest decline since May 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, when such deposits decreased by 72.22 trillion won ($48.5 billion).

Demand deposits allow customers to withdraw money at any time and include checking accounts and other accounts used for payments and short-term cash management.



freestar.config.enabled_slots.push({ placementName: "upi-com_incontent_reusable", slotId: "upi-com_incontent_reusable_92750" });

The balance fell by 22.47 trillion won ($15.1 billion) in January before rising for two consecutive months to 699.91 trillion won ($470.1 billion). It declined by 3.36 trillion won ($2.3 billion) in April and then increased for two months.

The total exceeded 700 trillion won for the first time and reached 722.29 trillion won ($485.2 billion) at the end of June.

Analysts said much of July's decline could be attributed to seasonal corporate cash movements.

Companies often place money in demand deposit accounts near the end of a quarter to manage financial ratios. The funds are then withdrawn and redeployed after quarterly or half-year financial statements are completed.

Companies also use the deposits to settle bills and make payments following the end of the reporting period.

Similar seasonal declines occurred in July 2024 and July 2025, when demand deposits decreased by 27.75 trillion won ($18.6 billion) and 17.49 trillion won ($11.7 billion), respectively.

This year's decline was considerably larger, however, partly because of increased stock market investment.

Individual investors continued buying shares during a recent correction in South Korea's benchmark Kospi index, absorbing some of the shares sold by foreign investors.

Foreign investors sold a net 10.83 trillion won ($7.3 billion) of Kospi-listed shares through Wednesday, while individual investors bought a net 6.18 trillion won ($4.2 billion).

The trend represented a reversal from June, when foreign investors purchased a net 47.03 trillion won ($31.6 billion) of shares and individual investors sold a net 39.54 trillion won ($26.6 billion).

Investor deposits held at securities companies, which are commonly viewed as money waiting to enter the stock market, also remain well above levels recorded at the beginning of the year.

Those deposits totaled 92.6 trillion won ($62.2 billion) on Jan. 15 and exceeded 130 trillion won ($87.3 billion) at the end of May.

They declined into the 120 trillion-won range after the Kospi fell sharply in late June and dropped to about 110 trillion won ($73.9 billion) in July. The level remains higher than it was at the beginning of the year.

Average daily Kospi trading volume by value nearly doubled from 27.06 trillion won ($18.2 billion) in January to 50.35 trillion won ($33.8 billion) in June.

"Corporate cash movements may have had an effect, but because the stock market decline began only recently, there is also a strong possibility that demand deposits held by individuals and companies moved into the stock market," said Kim Sang-bong, an economics professor at Hansung University.

Rising interest rates also encouraged customers to move cash from accounts offering immediate access into higher-yielding fixed-term deposits.



freestar.config.enabled_slots.push({ placementName: "upi-com_incontent_reusable", slotId: "upi-com_incontent_reusable_14019" });

The Bank of Korea raised its benchmark interest rate from 2.5% to 2.75% Thursday. The country's five largest banks had already increased interest rates on major fixed-term deposit products in May and June in anticipation of tighter monetary policy.

Interest rates on leading online fixed-term deposits with one-year maturities ranged from 2.9% to 3.3% annually Monday.

Fixed-term deposits at the five banks totaled 965.29 trillion won ($648.4 billion) as of Wednesday, up 15.9 trillion won ($10.7 billion), or 1.67%, from the end of June.

It was their largest monthly increase since May 2025.

-- Reported by Asia Today; translated by UPI
